title: Review: talking about your people
why: This review wraps up the unit on the people around us: it brings together possessives, describing people, gustar and direct object pronouns, with nothing new. You should be able to introduce your family and friends, say what they like and how often you see them, before moving on to the present tense in motion.

{"lessons": ["

Introducing your people

This lesson doesn't introduce anything new: it brings together everything you need to talk about your family and friends. Start with the possessives.

PossessiveExamples
mi / mismi hermano, mis primas
tu / tustu madre, tus abuelos
su / sussu marido (de Ana), sus hijos (de usted)
nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, nuestrasnuestra familia, nuestros padres
vuestro, vuestra, vuestros, vuestrasvuestro piso, vuestras hijas

A reminder of the traps: no article (mi casa), an -s when the thing owned is plural (mi becomes mis), and su, which covers “his, her, its, their, your.”

Describing: ser, tener, llevar

VerbTo talk aboutExample
seridentity, looks, personalityMi tía es baja y muy alegre.
tenerhair, eyes, beard; ageTiene el pelo blanco y setenta años.
llevarclothes, glassesSiempre lleva un sombrero.
estarhow someone is right now, locationHoy está cansada. Está en Cádiz.
Mi hermano mayor se llama Javier. Es alto, moreno y tiene barba. Es muy trabajador, pero un poco serio. Vive en Valencia con su pareja.My older brother's name is Javier. He's tall, dark-haired and has a beard. He's very hardworking, but a bit serious. He lives in Valencia with his partner.

To talk about resemblance: Me parezco a mi padre, Mi hermana y yo nos parecemos mucho. And don't forget the personal a before a person: Conozco a su hermano. Remember too that age goes with tener: Spanish “has” seventy years where English “is” seventy.

", "

What they like

With gustar, encantar and interesar, the thing that's liked is the subject: the verb agrees with it.

Who?PronounVerbWhat?
A mi padrelegustael fútbol.
A mis primoslesencantanlos videojuegos.
A nosotrosnosinteresala historia.
¿A vosotrososgustacocinar?

Three traps to watch for

  • The pronoun is required even when you name the person: A Lucía le gusta, never “a Lucía gusta.”
  • Plural if the thing that's liked is plural: Le gustan los perros.
  • Before one or more infinitives, singular: Le gusta leer y pasear.

Reacting

Someone saysYou answer
A mi madre le encanta bailar.A la mía también. / A la mía no.
A mi hijo no le gustan las verduras.A mi hija tampoco. / A mi hija sí.

In the right-hand column, la mía means “mine”: you can understand it without using it yet. To react simply, say A mi madre también.

", "

Avoiding repetition

When you talk about your people, you quickly end up repeating the same names. Direct object pronouns go before the conjugated verb:

PersonPronounExample
mi abueloloLo visito los domingos.
mi sobrinalaLa veo poco.
mis primoslosLos llamo todas las semanas.
mis amigaslasLas invito a cenar el sábado.
yo / túme / teMi madre me llama todos los días. ¿Te llama tu madre?
nosotros / vosotrosnos / osMis tíos nos invitan. ¿Os invitan a vosotros?
Tengo una sobrina, Ana. La quiero mucho, pero la veo poco porque vive en Lugo. Le encanta dibujar y siempre me da sus dibujos.I have a niece, Ana. I love her very much, but I don't see her much because she lives in Lugo. She loves drawing and she always gives me her drawings.

Notice the difference in this text between la quiero (direct object: I love her) and le encanta (with encantar: she loves it, it delights her).

What about Mexico?

You'll meet lots of Latin American Spanish speakers in Spain. A few differences to recognize:

  • In Mexico, people often say mis papás and mi mamá for “my parents” and “my mom.”
  • In Latin America, vosotros isn't used: people say ustedes (¿A ustedes les gusta?) even among friends.
  • No leísmo: for a man, it's always lo (Lo conozco).

You can stick with the Spanish of Spain: mis padres, vosotros, os. You'll be understood everywhere.
